title: Dick Gibson as jazz patron and philanthropist
summary: Hinton and Leeman credit Dick Gibson for his private jazz parties in Colorado, which Leeman has played every year, and for helping down-and-out musicians and reviving Joe Venuti.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: We've covered a tremendous amount of stuff here tonight. We're in our fourth hour, and I think by now, we can mention that we established the fact that you are one of the mainstays of jazz drummers in America and in the world. Now let's get to this one thing. Jazz musicians in the last few years, have been subsidized by very wealthy people; they have taken it upon themselves to want to see us and hear us, appreciate us, and sort of subsidize jazz, which has kept you and I alive.
Right -- and some of these people are dead.

And these people have been most gracious, and I don't think the world knows about them or have accepted them. They're not even interested in being accepted -- they are just Americans who believe in this truly great art of American jazz, and I think we can start with Richard Gibson.
Richard Gibson, started almost from the ground floor, number one.
That's right.
And helping me personally, among other things -- not only promoting jazz, but he went for a load of money and kept up his, and didn't let down on it.
He used to have private jazz parties for the last how many years?
This will be the 17th coming up.
Seventeen years.
I'm the only one that made them all.
You made them all?
Yes.
So Richard Gibson -- Dick Gibson has been giving jazz parties in Denver, in Aspen, and in Vail, Colorado, at the Broadmore Hotel, for how many years?
This will be the 17th year. Just count 17 from nine -- '62, I think.
Okay, but in every aspect of it, you have made every one that he's had.
That's right -- I've been fortunate enough.
You've never been fortunate, because you have honestly deserved this. You have been the mainstay of the jazz drummers --
I have a very strong love for it. Aside from music, for what they've done.
Well, I'm not talking about that. This
is your life. But it's all tieing in.
I don't want to interrupt you, so if you want to talk, I'll let you talk.
Well, he's single handedly done -- started the ball rolling, and done more. He has done more for musicians personally, along with the musical things.
Jazz musicians.
Yes, and he's helped musicians more than people know.
We'd like to mention that.

It wasn't much publicized. He's helped people financially that are down and out, he's a philanthropist in his own right. Whenever he can afford to be, and sometimes when he can't afford to be. He's helped people that were down and out get back on their feet, he pulled people out of a hat, he brought Joe Venuti back to the public.
(CUT)
(END OF PROCEEDINGS AS RECORDED)
